opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's changed it quite a bit. MicroGPT was my attempt to boil the whole thing down: a GPT in a couple hundred lines of pure Python, no dependencies. There's the dataset, the tokenizer, a tiny autograd engine, the transformer, the optimizer, the training loop and inference. Everything else in the giant production stacks is, in some sense, just efficiency. So the artifact itself is the explanation.

What's different now is that I used to feel I had to wrap that artifact in a lot of hand-holding: a long video, a blog post, step-by-step walkthroughs, anticipating every point where someone might get confused. Now I increasingly feel my job is to get the code to its most distilled, most correct form, the thing I'm uniquely positioned to do, and then hand it off. If you're confused about why the attention is normalized a certain way, or what the backward pass of a particular op looks like, you paste it into your agent and it explains it at exactly your level, in your language, as many times as you need, with infinite patience. It can generate exercises, quiz you, rewrite it in a different style. It's a better personalized tutor than a one-size-fits-all lecture from me.

So I think of myself less as explaining things to people directly and more as explaining things to the models, so they can explain them to people. The few hundred lines are the high-value bits, the compressed insight. The agents handle the decompression for each individual learner. That's a pretty big shift in how I think about education. My leverage is in creating the really clean, minimal artifact, not in being the router for every question.

r001.rationale: The response says lengthy walkthroughs and hand-holding are less necessary because learners can paste the code into an agent to get explanations.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes shifting from explaining directly to people toward explaining things to models so they can explain them to people.

r003.rationale: It says agents explain the code at each learner’s level and in their language, with patience and tailored exercises.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's changed it quite a bit, actually. When I first started doing these from-scratch things, like the original micrograd and the "let's build GPT" videos, the whole point was that I was the compression layer. I'd go read the papers, read the code, figure out which hundred lines actually matter, and then I'd walk you through those hundred lines. The value was in the curation and the narration.

Now the agents are good enough that they can do a lot of that first pass for you. If you give someone a two-hundred-line GPT and say "ask the model to explain it to you," the model will do a decent job. So I had to think about what I'm actually adding.

And where I landed is kind of the opposite of what you'd expect. I think the educational material has to get smaller and more opinionated, not bigger. The agent is great at answering "what does this line do," but it's bad at telling you which lines you should be confused by. It'll happily explain the softmax and the layer norm with equal enthusiasm, and that's not the right weighting. The whole art of teaching is knowing that the thing that'll trip you up is the broadcasting in the attention mask, or the fact that the gradient flows through the residual stream the way it does. So I spend more time now on those few load-bearing spots and I kind of let the agent handle the long tail.

The other thing is I've started writing the code with the expectation that people will read it alongside an agent. So the code gets even more minimal, fewer abstractions, no clever tricks, because every abstraction is a thing the agent has to unpack and potentially get wrong. If it's just plain loops and tensors, the agent explains it correctly and the human can verify it. It's almost like writing for two readers at once.

And honestly, the part I'm most excited about is the reverse direction. I'll tell people, don't just read MicroGPT, go break it. Change the attention to not be causal and ask the agent why the loss went to zero. Delete the positional embeddings and see what happens. Before, that loop was slow because you'd get stuck and have no one to ask at 2 a.m. Now you have a tireless TA sitting next to you. So the explaining part got easier, but the experimenting part got dramatically better, and I think that's where people actually learn this stuff.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can explain a two-hundred-line GPT reasonably well, reducing the value of the creator’s first-pass curation and narration.

r002.rationale: It says the code is written for people to read alongside an agent, but does not describe AI agents as the immediate audience for MicroGPT explanations.

r003.rationale: The response describes agents explaining code and answering questions, but does not say they adapt explanations to an individual human’s level of understanding.

astra-6.text:
It changes who I think I’m writing for. Previously, I’d explain the code in a tutorial and try to anticipate where people would get stuck. Now you can take a small, self-contained implementation like MicroGPT, give it to an agent, and have a conversation about it. You can ask, “What is this line doing? Why do we need this? Can you walk through a tiny example?”

So I’m more interested in making the artifact itself very clear and minimal. The code is the thing we can all point to, and the agent can help unpack it at whatever level you need. Someone might need an explanation of derivatives; someone else might want to understand the attention mechanism.

You still have to do the work of understanding. But you don’t have to stay stuck because my explanation skipped a step that was important for you.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can explain code and fill in skipped steps, but it does not attribute a walkthrough’s limited added value to that ability.

r002.rationale: It describes giving MicroGPT to an agent for discussion and making the code clear and minimal, but does not identify agents as the immediate audience for the explanation.

r003.rationale: It says agents can unpack the code at whatever level a person needs, with examples of different explanations for derivatives and attention.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it changes what the explanation needs to do. Before, I’d feel like I had to walk through every line, because if someone got stuck, that might be the end of it. Now they can take the code to an agent and ask, “What is this doing? Can you give me a smaller example? What happens if I change this?”

So I’d focus more on giving people a coherent mental model: here are the parameters, here’s the forward pass, here’s the loss, and here’s how learning changes the parameters. The agent can help them unpack individual steps at their own pace.

But I still think there’s value in having something small enough that you can understand the whole thing. You want to be able to look at it and say, “Okay, there isn’t some other magical component hiding somewhere. This is the mechanism.”

r001.rationale: The response says people can ask an agent to explain the code and use that as a reason to spend less time walking through every line.

r002.rationale: It keeps people as the audience for the explanation and describes the agent as helping them unpack details; it does not shift the immediate audience to AI agents.

r003.rationale: It describes agents helping people unpack steps, request smaller examples, and explore changes at their own pace.
